content: The Campaign for Access to Essential Medicines is an international initiative launched by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) to improve the availability of essential medicines in developing countries. These essential medicines are critical for treating infectious diseases such as malaria, sleeping sickness, and tuberculosis, which are rare in developed nations but prevalent in poorer regions. However, these drugs are often prohibitively expensive, out of production, or poorly understood. The lack of research into diseases that predominantly affect the world's impoverished populations is referred to as the 10-90 gap, highlighting the disparity where only 10% of global health research is directed toward diseases affecting 90% of the world's poor. This gap exists because pharmaceutical companies rarely find it profitable to develop drugs for these conditions. While some countries have enacted legislation to encourage the development of essential medicines, such as orphan drug laws in the United States, MSF launched this campaign in November 1999 to raise awareness of the issue. The campaign was funded in part by the prize money from MSF's 1999 Nobel Peace Prize. The campaign advocates for the production of generic antiretroviral drugs to treat AIDS patients and supports efforts to pressure governments to compel pharmaceutical companies to lower drug prices. In 2001, MSF facilitated an agreement with the Brazilian Ministry of Health, along with research and production entities Fiocruz and FarManguinhos, to produce affordable generic antiretroviral drugs for use in low-income countries. Malaria Malaria remains a significant health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, which accounts for 90% of global malaria-related deaths. Although inexpensive drugs like chloroquine and sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine are available, resistance to these medications has emerged in many severely affected regions. MSF is urging governments to invest in the development of artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), which has proven to be highly effective. Leishmaniasis Leishmaniasis is a rare disease in developed countries but often occurs in epidemic proportions in poorer nations such as Sudan and Bangladesh. Despite its severity, it receives little international attention. The disease manifests in four forms—visceral leishmaniasis (VL or kala-azar), cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL), and diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL). VL, MCL, and DCL are particularly difficult to treat, especially when co-occurring with HIV infection. While pentavalent antimony (sodium stibogluconate) is a relatively inexpensive treatment, resistance to this drug is increasing. MSF is advocating for increased research and development of new therapies. Sleeping Sickness Sleeping sickness, or human African trypanosomiasis, is currently epidemic in Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Sudan, though it is also widespread in other parts of Africa. For advanced cases, the primary treatment is melarsoprol, a highly toxic and increasingly ineffective drug. In 2000, MSF launched a major effort to pressure pharmaceutical companies to enhance research and development of alternative treatments, such as eflornithine and nifurtimox. Other Diseases Epidemics of meningococcal meningitis can be controlled through large-scale vaccination campaigns when detected early. However, this requires maintaining expensive stockpiles of vaccines during epidemic seasons. MSF and the World Health Organization (WHO) are negotiating with pharmaceutical companies to reduce vaccine costs and to promote research into long-term immunization strategies and improved treatments. Tuberculosis (TB), though largely under control in developed countries, continues to kill millions in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Existing vaccines and drug therapies for TB are decades old. MSF is advocating for increased research into new vaccines and for reducing the cost of treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Current TB treatment regimens, which involve strict adherence to drugs like isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide, are challenging for patients to follow. Non-compliance often leads to the emergence of MDR-TB. Other conditions, such as Buruli ulcer, require surgical excision of infected tissue, while trachoma necessitates a combination of surgery (in cases of trichiasis) and complex tetracycline treatment. Many of these diseases, including tuberculosis, frequently occur as opportunistic infections in individuals with HIV, further complicating treatment efforts.
